chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Life of an ESOP

lessons.title: Exercising Your Options: Paying the Strike Price and Receiving Shares

children.text: Vesting is free. Exercising is not. This is the step where an ESOP stops being a line in an offer letter and starts demanding money from your bank account, often at the worst possible time.
Exercising

means telling the company you want the shares, paying the exercise price, and receiving those shares in your name. Two things happen in the same week: money leaves you, and a tax bill arrives. Nothing comes in unless you can sell.

markDefs.definition: The act of using a vested option: you pay the exercise price to the company and receive the corresponding shares.

body.text: Exercising converts an option into a share, and a paper gain into a real tax liability. Plan the cash before you sign the exercise form, not after.

children.text: The Payoff You Are Buying Into

An employee stock option behaves exactly like a long call option on your company, except you paid no premium for it. Below the exercise price it is worth nothing. Above it, every rupee of share value is yours.

body.caption: Ritika’s option at an exercise price of ₹18. The premium is zero because she was granted the option rather than buying it, so her breakeven is the exercise price itself.

children.text: That is the whole appeal of an ESOP, and also its trap. The diagram says nothing about when you can sell, or about the tax that lands the moment you exercise.
What Actually Happens, Step by Step

body.caption: The exercise process at a typical Indian company

cells: Confirm vested quantity and the exercise deadline on your ESOP platform or with HR
Maintains the vesting record, often on a platform such as Qapita, Hissa or Carta
Submit an exercise notice for a specific number of vested options
Verifies the request against your grant
Receives the money into its share application account
Board or committee allots shares and updates the register of members
Shares arrive in your demat account, or you receive a certificate
Files the required returns with the Registrar of Companies
See a lower salary credit that month
Deducts TDS on the perquisite from your salary and deposits it

children.text: Step 4 is the one people underestimate. Until the board allots and your name enters the
register of members
, you are not a shareholder. After it, you are, with the right to receive dividends and to vote, subject to what the scheme and the articles allow.

markDefs.definition: The register of members: the company’s official list of shareholders. Your name appearing here is what makes you a shareholder.

children.text: The Cash Squeeze, With Real Numbers
Ritika has 3,000 vested options at ₹18. Her company’s
fair market value
is now ₹250 a share. She exercises the lot.

markDefs.definition: Fair Market Value: the value of one share on a given date, taken from the exchange for listed shares and from a registered valuer for unlisted ones.

body.latex: \text{Perquisite value} = (\text{FMV on exercise date} - \text{Exercise price}) \times \text{Options exercised}
body.caption: (₹250 minus ₹18) × 3,000 = ₹6,96,000 added to her salary income for the year.

children.text: That gain is a
perquisite
, taxed as salary under Section 17(1)(d) read with Section 17(5)(h) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [Section 17(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961]. Her employer must deduct
TDS
on it, which means it comes straight out of her next salary credit. Assume she is in the 30% slab, so 31.2% with cess, and ignore surcharge.

markDefs.definition: A non-cash benefit from employment that is taxed as part of salary. The discount you get when you exercise options is one.
Tax Deducted at Source: tax your employer withholds from your salary and deposits with the government on your behalf.

stats.label: Tax on the perquisite
stats.context: 31.2% of ₹6,96,000, deducted from salary as TDS

stats.label: Total cash she must find
stats.context: Before she receives a single rupee from the shares

stats.label: Value of shares received
stats.context: Real value, but not necessarily sellable

body.text: If the company is unlisted and has no buyback window, Ritika has just paid ₹2,71,152 in cash for shares she cannot sell. The gain is taxed now; the money may arrive years later, or never. This is the single hardest part of Indian ESOPs.

body.title: Size the Perquisite
body.prompt: Ritika exercises 3,000 options at an exercise price of ₹18 when the fair market value is ₹250. What amount is added to her salary income as a perquisite?
body.explanation: (₹250 minus ₹18) × 3,000 = ₹6,96,000. Note that this is taxed whether or not she sells anything, which is why the cash planning matters.

children.text: Where the Fair Market Value Comes From
You cannot argue with the fair market value, so it helps to know how it is set.
Listed shares:

the average of the opening and closing price on the exercise date. If the share trades on both the NSE and the BSE, the exchange with the higher volume in that share is used. If there was no trading that day, the closing price on the nearest earlier date applies.
Unlisted shares:
a valuation certified by a SEBI-registered Category I merchant banker, dated no more than 180 days before the exercise date.

body.label: Validity of a merchant banker valuation for unlisted ESOP exercises
body.context: The valuation date cannot be more than 180 days before the date you exercise.

body.text: For an unlisted company this creates a real timing lever. Exercising just before a big up round, while an older and lower valuation is still valid, can reduce the perquisite sharply. Ask your finance team when the current valuation expires.

children.text: Cashless Exercise: Only If You Can Sell
A
cashless exercise
, also called sell to cover, solves the cash problem by selling shares at the moment of issue. It works when there is a buyer: a listed company, a company-run buyback, or a secondary sale window.

markDefs.definition: An exercise route where shares are sold at the same time as they are issued, so the sale proceeds fund the exercise price and the tax.

children.text: Ritika needs ₹2,71,152: ₹54,000 for the exercise price and ₹2,17,152 for the tax. At ₹250 a share she must sell 1,085 shares, which raises ₹2,71,250.
She keeps 1,915 shares, worth ₹4,78,750 at the same price, and has paid nothing out of her own pocket. The cost is that she now owns fewer shares, so less of the future upside.

Some companies offer a same-day sale of the entire holding instead, which converts the whole grant to cash and leaves you with no shares at all. That is a decision about how much company risk you want, not a formality.

body.title: How Many Shares Must She Sell?
body.prompt: Ritika needs ₹2,71,152 to cover the exercise price and the tax. Her shares can be sold at ₹250 each. What is the smallest whole number of shares she must sell?
body.explanation: ₹2,71,152 ÷ ₹250 = 1,084.6, so she must sell 1,085 shares, raising ₹2,71,250. That leaves her 1,915 shares worth ₹4,78,750.

children.text: Exercise Now or Later?

columns.label: Exercise early
points: Perquisite is small while the fair market value is still close to the exercise price
The holding period for capital gains starts sooner
You become a shareholder and stop worrying about the exercise deadline
But your money is locked in an illiquid, risky asset
And you pay tax on a gain you may never realise

columns.label: Wait
points: No cash out, no tax, no risk until you act
You can exercise when a liquidity event is visible
But the perquisite grows with every valuation increase
You must still exercise before the expiry date
And a short post-exit window can force your hand

body.title: The Unlisted Exercise Decision
body.question: Farhan has vested options in an unlisted company with no buyback so far. Exercising all of them costs ₹1.4 lakh plus ₹4.6 lakh of perquisite tax. His exercise window runs for another four years. What is the most sensible first question to ask?
options: What is the share price today?
Is there any realistic route to selling these shares, and when?
Can I exercise in instalments to spread the tax?
Will the company list this year?
body.explanation: All four are worth asking, but liquidity comes first. Paying ₹6 lakh for an asset with no visible route to a buyer is a concentrated bet on one company, funded by your savings and taxed immediately. Option C is a good follow-up, since partial exercise is usually allowed and spreads both cash and tax.

body.title: Name the Tax Event
body.textWithBlank: The gap between fair market value and exercise price on the day you exercise is taxed as a salary ___ , and your employer deducts TDS on it.
body.explanation: It is treated as a benefit received from employment, added to your salary income for that year, and taxed at your slab rate. The later increase in value, from exercise to sale, is capital gains instead.

body.title: Two Weeks to Decide
body.scenario: Meenakshi is leaving a Bengaluru fintech after five years. She has 12,000 vested options at an exercise price of ₹25. The latest valuation puts the share at ₹210. Her scheme gives her 30 days from her last working day to exercise, after which the options lapse. She has ₹12 lakh in savings, an EMI of ₹42,000 a month, and the company has run one buyback in five years.
body.prompt: How should she think about this, and what are her options?
body.modelAnswer: First, the numbers. Exercising everything costs 12,000 × ₹25 = ₹3,00,000, and the perquisite is 12,000 × ₹185 = ₹22,20,000, which at a 31.2% effective rate means about ₹6,92,640 of tax, so roughly ₹9.93 lakh in total against savings of ₹12 lakh. That would leave her with almost no emergency fund while carrying an EMI, in exchange for shares she may not be able to sell. Second, partial exercise. Most schemes allow her to exercise a part, so she could take a quantity she can comfortably fund, for instance a third, and let the rest lapse. Third, negotiation. It is worth asking in writing whether the exercise window can be extended, whether the company will include her in the next buyback, or whether it will facilitate a secondary sale. Companies do sometimes agree, especially for a five-year employee leaving on good terms. The wrong move is to fund the full exercise with borrowed money on the assumption that a liquidity event is coming.

children.text: After You Exercise
You now hold shares, usually in a
demat account
, and your name is on the register of members. Watch for three things: any
lock-in

the scheme imposes, the trading window rules if the company is listed and you are an insider, and your own concentration risk. Your salary and a large part of your savings now depend on the same company.

markDefs.definition: A dematerialised account that holds shares electronically, the same kind of account you would open with Zerodha or any other broker.
A period after allotment during which the scheme or the law does not allow you to sell the shares.

cards.definition: The form telling the company how many vested options you want to convert.
The taxable salary benefit equal to FMV minus exercise price, times options exercised.
Tax your employer withholds from salary, including on the ESOP perquisite.
Selling some or all shares at the moment of issue to fund the exercise price and tax.
The official shareholder list. Your name here makes you a shareholder.
The SEBI-registered valuer whose certificate sets FMV for unlisted shares, valid for up to 180 days.

points: Exercising means paying the exercise price and receiving shares. Vesting alone gives you nothing to hold.
Two cash events hit together: the exercise price, and tax on the perquisite deducted from your salary.
Ritika paid ₹54,000 to exercise and ₹2,17,152 in tax, so ₹2,71,152 left her account before any money came in.
FMV is the average of the opening and closing price for listed shares, and a merchant banker valuation no more than 180 days old for unlisted ones.
Cashless exercise solves the cash problem only when a buyer exists.
Exercising early keeps the perquisite small; waiting keeps your money safe. Neither is right for everyone.
Before exercising in an unlisted company, ask how and when you could ever sell.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Tax rates used here are illustrative, ignore surcharge and assume the 30% slab. Your own slab, scheme terms and circumstances will differ, so consult a qualified professional before exercising.
